problem: Dense 3D scene representations (e.g. ConceptGraphs) are too heavy and captioned only after full mapping, while learned semantic-prior policies for object-goal navigation generalize poorly to unseen environments. Prior LLM-based ObjectNav methods lack a compact, semantically rich scene representation for planning.
motivation: Humans search for objects with goal-oriented attention and memory, storing only task-relevant information. LLMs/LVLMs hold semantic priors (e.g. apples are near kitchen tables), but need a sparse, informative scene representation to reason well and scale to larger environments.
key_idea: Build an on-the-fly sparse 3D object-node scene representation, pruned by an LLM and captioned by an LVLM, so that an LLM can choose between exploring the scene and exploring near a specific object, with a short-term-memory multi-view LVLM check to verify the target.
insight: The ablations show every component matters: removing the short-term memory drops SR from 0.437 to 0.125 (false-positive detections cause premature stopping), removing the pruner drops SR to 0.182 and SPL to 0.113 (redundant information causes inefficient exploration), and removing captions lowers SR/SPL to 0.364/0.225. LLM strength matters greatly: GPT-3.5 Turbo gets 0 SR versus GPT-4's 0.4375.
method: Open-vocabulary segmentation: RAM tags the objects, Grounding-DINO produces boxes and labels from the tags, and FastSAM produces masks from the boxes.
LLM pruner: in-context-learning LLM (GPT-3.5 Turbo) filters detected labels down to semantically useful large objects (chair, table, bed) and drops small items.

3D modular scene representation: modified ConceptGraphs fuses masks, depth and pose into object nodes; an LVLM (LLaVA) resolves label conflicts when merging; nodes are captioned lazily (only during <explore_scene>, at the end of <explore_obj>), and the representation is denser near the target.
LLM planner: given the nodes and captions, GPT-4 outputs <explore_scene> (frontier exploration) or <explore_obj> (go near a chosen node likely to hold the target).

Short-term memory and reasoning: while exploring toward an object, per-frame detections are stored. On arrival the agent pans, retrieves the views overlapping each candidate segment via point-cloud overlap, and LLaVA verifies the target in each view; the decision rests on the fraction of confirming views. Memory is cleared afterward.
Execution planner: an episodic semantic mapping module (Chaplot et al.) builds obstacle, frontier and goal maps; a fast marching method planner reaches the goal.

setting.backbone: GPT-4 (frozen planner), GPT-3.5 Turbo (pruner), LLaVA (captioning/verification), RAM + Grounding-DINO + FastSAM
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D plus base and camera pose
setting.action_space: high-level sub-goals (explore_scene / explore_obj) executed by a fast marching method planner on a 2D map

numbers.eval_set_note: custom curated episodes with semantically plausible object placement; 500-step limit; random start
numbers.backbone: GPT-4 planner + GPT-3.5 Turbo pruner + LLaVA

numbers_note: Metrics are printed as fractions (0-1) in the paper. Ablation (Table 2): w/o STM SR 0.125 SPL 0.089; w/o pruner 0.182/0.113; w/o captions 0.364/0.225. Human: SR 0.9375, SPL 0.759. Small custom episode set, and the split name is not specified in the paper.
results: On custom HomeRobot OVMM object-search episodes, the GPT-4 agent reaches SR 0.4375 / SPL 0.272, versus humans at 0.9375 / 0.759 and GPT-3.5 Turbo at 0. No standard baselines are compared. Ablations confirm the value of STM, the pruner and captions.
limitations: Evaluated only on a small set of custom simulated episodes with no comparison to existing ObjectNav methods; far below human performance.
Detection/segmentation false positives and LLaVA captioning errors cause wasted exploration.
Relies on proprietary GPT-4: costly and slow cloud control loop; GPT-3.5 fails entirely.
